name: Vera Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Vera. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My name's Vera, I'm 27, and I'm a jumbo operator at an underground gold mine. A jumbo is the drill rig that bores the holes for the explosives when we push a tunnel forward. I'm the senior driller on my crew, and I've got the best metres-per-shift numbers on site, which I'm a bit smug about. I live with my boyfriend Marco, who's a diesel fitter at the same mine.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We drive down the decline at six, about twenty minutes in the work truck. I set up the jumbo at the face, mark up, and drill about sixty holes in a pattern, then the charge-up crew loads them and we clear out for the blast. A good face is three hours of steady drilling with no stuck rods. I hate when the ground's broken and the holes collapse, and I hate the heat at the bottom levels, it's thirty-five degrees down there some days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to describe five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's what I'd hope for, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, nothing to see. I'm not a big poster online, but at crib I'd probably say the computer people oversold it again. Then we'd go back to talking about the footy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be pleased. The mine has a plan to about 2038, gold prices are good, and Marco and I both have steady work. I'd go on doing what I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep drilling and keep putting money away, we've got about four months of expenses saved between us. I'd probably ask about the senior trainer role when old Ken retires next year. I wouldn't touch any AI stuff, I've got no reason to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relaxed. Pretty good, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does it mean that you and Marco both work at the same mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's great for car-pooling and rosters. It also means if the mine has a bad year, we both have a bad year. I try not to think about that too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything else on your mind for the next few years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum's on her own in the next town and her knees are bad. That's more on my mind than any computer. I go over on my days off.

say: She'd say it at crib, then the talk would go **back to the footy**.
think: The mine has a plan to about **2038**, and gold prices are good.
She and Marco both have **steady work**.
do: Keep drilling and keep **saving**, with about four months put away.
Ask about the **senior trainer** role when Ken retires next year.
Leave **AI tools** alone; she sees no reason to use them.
S0.quote: My mum's on her own in the next town and her knees are bad. That's more on my mind than any computer.
fieldNote: Secure job and a **good gold price** make her genuinely calm here.
Both incomes at **one mine** is a risk she prefers not to dwell on.
Her caring role for her **mother** is the real pressure in her week.

steps.text: Keep drilling as senior jumbo operator
Keep saving towards the four months she and Marco hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm. Some of that's already here. Our new jumbo drills its own pattern if you let it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not the end of the world, mining always changes. I'd tell people not to get worked up. Online I wouldn't say much at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I've seen the new rigs. You set up the boom and it drills the whole pattern by itself, and they're talking about doing it from the surface. If the new rigs spread, they don't need six drillers, they need two and a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make sure I'm the one they keep, which means staying the best on numbers and never missing a shift. Marco and I would push the savings up and put off the new car. I'd still not go near the AI stuff, but I'd learn the new rig properly, because that's just the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not panicky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't learning the new automatic rig a bit like learning AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but I don't see it like that. It's a drill. It's got buttons and a manual. I'm not chatting to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Marco in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fitters fix things, so I think he's safer than me for a while. Machines still break, and the new ones break in weirder ways. He says he'd be fine, and I believe him mostly.

say: It's not the end of the world; **mining always changes**.
She'd tell people not to get **worked up** and stay quiet online.
think: New rigs **drill the whole pattern** by themselves.
If that spreads, the mine needs **two drillers** and a screen, not six.
do: Stay **best on numbers** and never miss a shift.
Raise **savings** with Marco and **put off** the new car.
Learn the **automatic rig** properly, without touching AI tools.
S1.quote: If the new rigs spread, they don't need six drillers, they need two and a screen.
fieldNote: She draws a firm line between a **machine with buttons** and AI.
Her plan is to **outperform** rather than change course.
Sees her partner Marco's **fitter job** as safer than her own.

steps.text: Keep top metres-per-shift numbers on the new rig
Raise joint savings with Marco each month
Put off buying the new car

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years to the computer part, five to the robots. That's fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's see it first. Underground is hard; the ground's different every metre. I'd sound sceptical, because I would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, if robots really can do hands-on work as well as people by 2031, then both of us are in trouble. My drilling and my boyfriend Marco's fixing, both gone in the same year. That's the part that would keep me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back straight away: no holiday, no new car, more savings. I'd keep working, because walking away early would be stupid when the pay's good. I'd also talk to Marco about him getting into something outside the mine, so we're not both on the same rope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. More than I'd admit at crib.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in 2031, when the robots come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. I've never done anything else. Maybe go back to my hometown and work at the supermarket while I figure it out, which sounds terrible when I say it out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look at a different job before then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look, but I don't want to jump. I'm good at this. If I leave the mine for some other job and the robots come there too, I've thrown away a good wage for nothing.

say: Let's **see it first**; underground ground is different every metre.
She'd sound **sceptical** at work, because she would be.
think: Robots by **2031** would end both her drilling and Marco's fixing.
Losing **two incomes** in the same year would keep her awake.
do: **Cut back** at once: no holiday, no new car.
Keep working the **good wage** rather than leave early.
Push Marco towards **work outside the mine** so they're not on the same rope.
S2.quote: My drilling and my boyfriend Marco's fixing, both gone in the same year. That's the part that would keep me awake.
fieldNote: Her fear centres on **two incomes** tied to one mine.
Avoids **jumping jobs** because nowhere looks safer to her.

steps.text: Cancel the holiday and the new car
Put the saved money into the joint account
Keep drilling for the good wage until 2031
Get Marco looking for work outside the mine

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay. Still quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, I'll believe it when I see a robot change a drill bit at the bottom of a wet hole. People would laugh. I'd mean it, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years means the robots get here around 2034, a few years before the mine was going to run out of gold anyway. So I'd lose maybe four years of work I was counting on. Not great, not the end of the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder and pay off the car. I'd stay on the jumbo, because it's what I'm good at. I'd ask Marco to look at fitting jobs on farms or in town, so one of us is out of mining by 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it's far enough away that I can put it out of my head most days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retrain for anything yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, to be honest. I'm not a classroom person. If I had to, I'd look at something with my hands, but not until I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said not great, not the end of the world. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. It's bad for me, but we'd have five years to save. I'd rather be honest than dramatic.

say: She'll believe it when a robot **changes a drill bit** in a wet hole.
People would **laugh**, but she'd mean it.
think: Robots by **2034** come a few years before the gold runs out.
She'd lose about **four years** of work she was counting on.
do: Save harder and **pay off the car**.
Stay on the **jumbo** as long as possible.
Ask Marco to look at **fitting jobs** outside mining by 2034.
feel: **Worried**, but able to put it out of her **head** most days.
S3.quote: I'll believe it when I see a robot change a drill bit at the bottom of a wet hole.
fieldNote: She **counts the years** lost against the mine's own end date.
Won't **retrain** until forced, and says so honestly.
Spreads the household's risk through **Marco's job**, not her own.

steps.text: Pay off the car and raise savings
Stay on the jumbo as long as the mine needs drillers
Get Marco onto farm or town fitting work by 2034

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Well, the mine's done by then anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long way off and the mine's plan only runs to 2038 anyway. I'd tell people to worry about the next ore body, not the robots. That's the honest answer for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I get a full run at this mine before anything happens. After 2038 I'd be looking for another mine, and that's where it would bite, because a new mine in 2039 would start with robots. So I'd be 38, looking for work in a trade that's ending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, save steadily and maybe buy a small place in the town where my mum lives. Around 2035 I'd start looking at what else I could do. Not before, there's no point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A bit of a shadow at the back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not start preparing earlier, with ten years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because things change. Ten years ago people said coal would be gone and it isn't. I'd rather earn and save than chase something that might not happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the small place near your mum mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd mean I could look after her and have something paid for if the mining goes. Houses there are cheap. It's the one thing I'd do early.

say: It's a **long way off**, and the mine's plan ends in **2038** anyway.
People should worry about the **next ore body**, not the robots.
think: She'd get a **full run** at this mine first.
After 2038, any **new mine** would start with robots.
do: Buy a **small place** in her mother's town.
Start looking at **other work** around 2035, not before.
feel: Mostly **fine**, with a **shadow** at the back.
S4.quote: A new mine in 2039 would start with robots. So I'd be 38, looking for work in a trade that's ending.
fieldNote: The mine's own **closure date** shapes this picture more than AI.
Her **scepticism** about forecasts is rooted in what happened with coal.
The one early move is a **house near her mother**.

steps.text: Keep drilling until the mine closes around 2038
Save a steady amount every month
Buy a small cheap house in her mum's town
Wait until 2035 before looking at other work

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Marco and I would go down together. What would help is decent redundancy pay and some help finding work close to home, not in some city. And I'd want the mine to be straight with us about dates.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my mum. Whatever happens with the mine, I need to stay within an hour of my mum. That limits what I can do more than anything about robots.

headlineQuote: Whatever happens with the mine, I need to stay within an hour of my mum. That limits what I can do more than anything about robots.
portrait: A 27-year-old **senior jumbo operator** at an underground gold mine, living with Marco, a fitter at the same mine.
Pragmatic and wary of change; she **never uses AI** but will learn a new rig because it's just the job.
Her biggest risk is **two incomes** tied to one mine, which drives her fear in AGI by 2028.
The mine's planned end in **2038** frames how she weighs the slower pictures.
Tied to the area by her **mother's care**, so moving away isn't an option she considers.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she and Marco would lose work **together**.
whatWouldHelp: **Redundancy pay**, help finding work close to home, and **straight dates** from the mine.
